title: Longest Palindromic Substring
directAnswer: Return the longest contiguous substring that reads the same forwards and backwards. Brute force checks every substring in O(n³). The interview-grade answer is expand-around-center: treat each index (and each gap between indices) as a possible palindrome center and grow outward while characters match — O(n²) time, O(1) space.

remember.pattern: Expand around center — every palindrome has a middle
rules: There are **2n − 1 centers**, not n — every gap *between* two characters is also a center (for even-length palindromes).
Expand **while** `s[l] == s[r]` and both pointers are in bounds; the answer is `s[l+1 : r]` *after* the loop overshoots by one.
Track only the **best start and length**, not the substring itself — slice once at the end to avoid O(n) copies inside the loop.
A DP table is also O(n²) but costs O(n²) **space** — expand-around-center is strictly better, so lead with it.
Manacher's algorithm is the O(n) answer; **name it, don't code it** unless explicitly pushed — it's rarely expected.
whenToUse: Find the longest / count palindromic substrings of a string
The property is symmetric and grows from a middle point outward
You can verify a candidate by walking two pointers from a center
n is small enough (≤ ~1000) that O(n²) passes comfortably
antiSignals: Subsequence, not substring → that's Longest Palindromic Subsequence (interval DP)
Need true O(n) under a tight constraint → Manacher's, not center expansion
Checking a single fixed string is a palindrome → just two pointers, no scan
Partitioning into palindromes → backtracking + palindrome DP
remember.takeaway: Palindromes are defined by their center, not their ends. The moment you anchor on the middle and grow outward, an O(n³) substring-enumeration problem collapses to O(n²) with no extra memory. The same center-expansion trick solves Palindromic Substrings (count) and underlies Manacher's.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you avoid the naive 'enumerate every substring and test it' and instead exploit the structural symmetry of a palindrome to prune the search to centers.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Forgetting even-length palindromes — only expanding from single-character centers, which misses 'abba'. Or rebuilding the substring inside the loop, turning O(n²) into O(n³).
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Derive 2n−1 centers out loud, track indices not strings, and name Manacher's O(n) as the theoretical ceiling without pretending you'd code it under time pressure.

problemStatement:
Given a string `s`, return **the longest palindromic substring** in `s`.

A **palindrome** is a string that reads the same forwards and backwards. A **substring** is a contiguous sequence of characters within the string.

If there are multiple answers of the same maximum length, returning any one of them is accepted.
constraints: s consists of only digits and English letters
The answer is always a contiguous substring, never a subsequence
At least one palindrome always exists (any single character)
understanding: Find the longest run of characters that mirrors itself around a center. 'Substring' means contiguous — you cannot skip characters. Every single character is trivially a palindrome of length 1, so an answer always exists.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Substring or subsequence?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Substring — contiguous. If it were a subsequence we'd be solving a different, interval-DP problem (LeetCode 516).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the comparison case-sensitive?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. 'Aa' is not a palindrome here; the constraint says raw digits and letters, no normalization.

clarifyingQuestions.question: If several palindromes tie for longest, which do I return?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Any one of them. I'll return the first maximal one I find, which keeps the bookkeeping simple.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large can the string get?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to 1000 characters, so O(n²) ≈ 10⁶ operations is comfortably fast. That tells me I don't need Manacher's O(n).

examples.explanation: "bab" is a palindrome of length 3. "aba" is also valid — either is accepted.
The longest palindrome is the even-length "bb". This is the case a single-center expansion would miss.
A single character is a palindrome of length 1.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Decide before coding. For n ≤ 1000, expand-around-center is the sweet spot of speed, space, and simplicity.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Check Every Substring
approaches.whenToMention: Say it first to anchor the complexity, then immediately note the wasted re-work that the optimal approach eliminates.
hints: The most literal reading: a palindrome is a substring, so enumerate every substring and test each one. How many substrings are there, and how long does one palindrome check take?
There are ~n²/2 substrings (choose a start and an end). Verifying one substring is a palindrome takes O(n) with two pointers.
Two nested loops pick start i and end j; a helper walks inward from both ends to confirm the palindrome. Track the longest valid (i, j).
approaches.complexityReasoning: O(n²) substrings × O(n) to verify each = O(n³). No auxiliary structure, so O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Enumerate every substring `s[i..j]`, check whether it is a palindrome with a two-pointer walk, and remember the longest one that passes.

**Why this is the honest starting point.** The problem literally says 'find a substring with property P'. The zero-insight version of any such problem is: list all substrings, test the property on each, keep the best. It's correct and trivial to reason about, which is exactly why it's worth stating before optimizing — it pins down the baseline you're about to beat.

**Where the waste lives.** The killer is that checking `s[i..j]` from scratch throws away everything you learned checking `s[i+1..j-1]`. A palindrome of length 7 *contains* a palindrome of length 5 at its core — but brute force re-verifies that core every single time. That redundant inner work is the O(n) factor we're paying on top of the O(n²) pairs, and it's precisely what the next approach removes.

**Why we don't ship it.** For n = 1000, O(n³) is 10⁹ operations — borderline TLE and clearly signalling you didn't see the structure. State it, give the complexity, then pivot: 'every palindrome is built around a center, so let's grow from centers instead of testing arbitrary endpoints.'
approaches.insight: The redundancy is the whole story: a palindrome and its inner palindrome share a center. Brute force ignores that shared structure and re-checks the middle over and over. Recognizing that overlap is the bridge to both expand-around-center and the DP table.

approaches.name: Expand Around Center (Optimal for n ≤ 1000)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'every palindrome has a center — grow from there' rather than 'use two pointers'.
hints: Brute force re-checks shared cores. What if you started AT the core instead? Every palindrome is symmetric around a middle point — anchor there and grow outward.
There are two kinds of centers: a single character (odd length, like 'aba') and a gap between two characters (even length, like 'abba'). That's 2n−1 centers total.
From each center, move two pointers outward while they stay in bounds and the characters match. The widest successful expansion across all centers is the answer.
approaches.complexityReasoning: 2n−1 centers, each expansion is at most O(n) → O(n²) time. We store only a start index and a length, so O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
For each of the `2n − 1` possible centers, push two pointers outward while the characters match and stay in bounds. Whenever an expansion beats the best length seen so far, record its start and length. Slice the answer out once at the end.

**The mental shift that unlocks this.** Brute force asks *'is this arbitrary substring a palindrome?'* — there are n²/2 substrings and verifying each is O(n). Expand-around-center flips the question: *'how far does the palindrome centered here reach?'* Because a palindrome is defined by symmetry around a midpoint, fixing the midpoint and growing is a single uninterrupted walk — the moment two characters disagree, no wider palindrome shares this center, so you stop. You never re-verify an inner core because you *built outward from* it.

**Why 2n − 1 centers and not n.** Odd-length palindromes ('aba') are centered on a character. Even-length palindromes ('abba') are centered on the *gap between* two characters — there is no single middle character. There are n character-centers and n−1 gap-centers, hence 2n − 1. Miss the gap-centers and you silently fail every even-length answer like 'cbbd' → 'bb'. The clean way to handle both is to call the same expand helper twice per index: once with `(i, i)` and once with `(i, i+1)`.

**Why we track indices, not the substring.** It's tempting to keep `best = s.substring(...)` inside the loop, but that copies up to O(n) characters every time you improve — and in the worst case ('aaaa...') you improve O(n) times, dragging the work back toward O(n³) on the allocation axis. Storing just `start` and `maxLen` keeps the inner loop O(1) per step; you materialize the string exactly once at the return.

**The ceiling, briefly.** Manacher's algorithm reuses palindrome information across centers to hit true O(n). It's worth *naming* so the interviewer knows you know it exists, but coding it from memory under pressure is a needless risk when n ≤ 1000 makes O(n²) trivially fast.
approaches.insight: The whole speedup comes from never throwing away the symmetric core. Brute force re-checks the middle of every candidate; center-expansion makes the middle the *starting point*, so each character pair is compared a bounded number of times. When a 'find the longest X substring' problem has a property that grows symmetrically (or monotonically) from a point, anchoring on that point and expanding is almost always the unlock.

pitfalls: Only calling expand(i, i) and skipping expand(i, i+1) — silently misses every even-length palindrome.
Returning r - l + 1 instead of r - l - 1 — forgetting the loop overshoots by one on both sides.
Storing the substring instead of (start, len) inside the loop — extra O(n) copies on each improvement.

commonMistakes: Only expanding from single-character centers, missing even-length palindromes like "bb".
Computing the palindrome length as r - l + 1 instead of r - l - 1 after the expansion overshoots.
Re-slicing the substring on every improvement instead of recording start and length once.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting even-length centers
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Expanding only from (i, i) handles odd palindromes ('aba') but never the gap between two characters, so 'cbbd' wrongly returns a length-1 answer instead of 'bb'.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong length after expansion
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The while loop stops only after l and r have each stepped one past the palindrome. The valid span is [l+1, r-1], whose length is (r-1)-(l+1)+1 = r - l - 1, not r - l + 1.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
while l >= 0 and r < len(s) and s[l] == s[r]:
    l -= 1
    r += 1
return r - l + 1   # overcounts by 2
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
while l >= 0 and r < len(s) and s[l] == s[r]:
    l -= 1
    r += 1
return r - l - 1

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Recovering start with the wrong formula
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Given a center i and final length, the left edge is i - (len - 1) / 2. Using len / 2 breaks for odd lengths and shifts the substring left by one.

patternNote: Center-Expansion for Palindromes. Whenever a problem hinges on contiguous symmetry around a midpoint, anchor on the 2n−1 centers and grow outward. Same engine powers Palindromic Substrings (counting) and is the brute-force baseline Manacher's optimizes.
